text: Testing shows the presence, not the absence, of bugs.
Quality is never an accident; it is always the result of intelligent effort.
Beware of bugs in the above code; I have only proved it correct, not tried it.
The bitterness of poor quality remains long after the sweetness of meeting the schedule is forgotten.
Shift-left testing: move quality checks earlier in the pipeline, when defects are cheapest to fix.
Exploratory testing is simultaneous learning, test design, and test execution.
Treat flaky tests as production bugs — they quietly erode trust in the entire suite.
Run a bug hunt pairing developers and testers: the fastest way to find and fix issues together.
1947: Grace Hopper's team found a moth stuck in the Harvard Mark II relay, coining the term "debugging".
1999: NASA lost the $327M Mars Climate Orbiter to a metric/imperial unit mismatch — a verification failure.
2000: The Y2K bug triggered a worldwide audit of two-digit year fields across every industry.
2002: ISTQB was founded to standardize software testing certification worldwide.
The Pareto principle applies to code: roughly 20% of a codebase is responsible for ~80% of its defects.
Rubber duck debugging: explaining a bug out loud to an inanimate object often reveals the fix.
A "regression" is a bug that reappears in code that used to work — hence "regression testing".
Most bugs are introduced when requirements change, not when code is originally written.
If debugging is the process of removing bugs, then programming must be the process of putting them in.
Quality means doing it right when no one is looking.
It's better to have fewer tests that matter than many tests that don't.
Automation is not a replacement for thinking; it is thinking made repeatable.
A tester is not the enemy; a tester is the mirror that shows you what you've missed.
Write a failing test first: red-green-refactor keeps every change small and verifiable.
Test the boundary values — most defects live at the edges of valid input, not the middle.
Use the test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a thin layer of E2E.
Separate test data from test logic so a single scenario can run against many datasets.
Log every flaky test with a ticket — never mute it and forget it.
1988: Cem Kaner published 'Testing Computer Software', one of the first books to define QA as a discipline.
2004: Selenium was created by Jason Huggins to automate browser testing at ThoughtWorks.
1996: The Therac-25 radiation overdoses became a landmark case study in why software safety testing matters.
2001: The Agile Manifesto was published, reshaping how teams integrate testing into development.
2010: The first World Quality Report began tracking QA trends across industries worldwide.
Smoke testing gets its name from plumbing: turn it on and check for smoke before deeper testing.
A 'heisenbug' is a bug that disappears the moment you try to observe or debug it.
Gherkin scenarios let non-technical stakeholders read test intent in plain language.
The five whys: asking 'why' five times usually traces a defect to its root cause.
Boundary value analysis catches more real-world bugs than almost any other technique — edges are where bugs hide.
